verdicts.text: With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
verdicts.evidence: The official AWS CDK README says CDK is used "to define cloud infrastructure in code and provision it through AWS CloudFormation." It also says the CLI can "synthesize artifacts such as AWS CloudFormation Templates," and that `cdk synth` "synthesizes an AWS CloudFormation template for your app," which is the template CloudFormation then deploys. That confirms the claim that CDK code generates an intermediate template.
verdicts.framing_note: CDK writes JSON templates. CloudFormation itself accepts templates in either YAML or JSON, so "YAML or JSON" is accurate for the CDK+CloudFormation pair.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Other sources describe AWS CDK as AWS-only because it synthesizes to CloudFormation. Encore says "CDK is AWS only. If you deploy to GCP or Azure, CDK doesn't help". SST's v3 migration docs point to Pulumi's "150+ other providers that allow you to build on any cloud" as what replaced CDK. Calling multi-cloud "nearly impossible" is a subjective summary, but it fits these facts.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Nearly impossible" is a bit strong: CloudFormation's registry supports some third-party resource types, but CDK is essentially AWS-only.

verdicts.text: SST (Serverless Stack) is a framework that aims to bridge the gap between application developers and infrastructure management.
verdicts.evidence: The SST homepage describes the framework as app-centric infrastructure tooling: "For whatever you build. Deploy everything your app needs with a single config." That broadly supports the claim's loose description, though the page never uses the phrase "bridge the gap", and the fetched text doesn't mention the "Serverless Stack" expansion.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim paraphrases the source's "Deploy everything your app needs with a single config" as "bridge the gap between application developers and infrastructure management". It is a subjective description, not a quote.

verdicts.text: SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own blog confirms that its earlier versions were built on CDK: Ion is a new engine whose components are "deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." A third-party post adds that "the first two versions of SST were basically the wrappers and enhancers of AWS CDK." Saying that CDK lets developers use TypeScript or Python is true, though CDK supports more languages than those two.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "TypeScript or Python" names only 2 of CDK's languages (it also supports JS, Java, C#, and Go). It could also be read as saying SST v2 users could write Python, but SST v2 apps were JS/TS only, so the wording is worth tightening.

verdicts.text: An embedded YouTube video with ID LXxJ9XMXC6o exists relating to CDK and CloudFormation limitations.
verdicts.evidence: L91 holds `{{< youtube "LXxJ9XMXC6o?rel=0" >}}`, right under the heading "## CDK and CloudFormation Limitations", so the embed is in the place the claim describes. I couldn't check with these tools whether the video is still live on YouTube or what it's actually about.
verdicts.framing_note: The embed is in place as described. It's still unchecked whether the video is live and actually covers CDK/CloudFormation limitations.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
verdicts.evidence: The claim is broadly accurate. The Pulumi AWS CDK comparison page backs it up: "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." This is well-known CDK behavior; I did not check it against AWS's own docs or product source.
verdicts.framing_note: Line 95 of the post says "the infrastructure code is essentially a code generator"; the extracted claim rewords this so that CDK and CloudFormation themselves are the generator. Strictly, CDK generates the JSON/YAML template and CloudFormation executes it, but the substance holds.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi docs page on CloudFormation comparison has a section anchored 'what-is-aws-cloudformation'.
verdicts.evidence: The CloudFormation comparison page has the heading "## What is AWS CloudFormation?" (L37). Hugo turns that into the anchor #what-is-aws-cloudformation, so the link will land on that section.

verdicts.text: SST's team expanded beyond AWS to explore other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and added support for new providers after moving to Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post confirms that the move to Pulumi was partly driven by wanting to support providers other than AWS: "there is now genuine demand from the SST community wanting to use Cloudflare". Its goal is to "create any kind of resource, in any cloud provider". SST v3 ships with AWS, Cloudflare and other providers. But no SST source mentions "on-premises infrastructure", so that part of the claim is unsupported.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: SST's post says 'any cloud provider' (Cloudflare, OpenAI, etc.), but the claim adds 'on-premises infrastructure', which the source never mentions
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'On-premises infrastructure' looks unlikely for SST, a serverless/cloud-focused framework. The blog may have added it on its own.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi docs page on AWS CDK comparison has a section anchored 'what-is-aws-cdk'.
verdicts.evidence: The target page has the heading "## What is AWS CDK?" at L35. Hugo turns that into the anchor `what-is-aws-cdk`, so the link resolves.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports extensibility through custom providers and dynamic components (dynamic providers).
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi docs describe dynamic resource providers as "lighter weight than custom providers" and point to bridged/native providers for more complex APIs, so both extension mechanisms exist. This confirms the capability, but the docs only link out to the non-dynamic provider types, so confidence is medium.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi doesn't use the term "dynamic components"; the official term is "dynamic providers" (supported only in TypeScript and Python). Consider rewording.

verdicts.text: Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide says that on `pulumi up` "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program." As each resource is constructed, "the language host sends a _resource registration_ request to the deployment engine and then continues executing the program." So the program runs directly during deployment and talks to the engine live, with no intermediate template step (unlike CDK, which synthesizes CloudFormation).
verdicts.framing_note: This is a docs page, not product source, so it can corroborate but isn't ground truth. GitHub search was rate-limited, so I couldn't check the engine source directly.

verdicts.text: A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't find this quote anywhere except the blog post under review, which doesn't count as evidence for itself. The talk is real: the PulumiUP 2024 agenda lists "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST" with "Dax Raad (Founding Engineer, SST)". But no transcript or other independent source confirms the exact wording or who said it.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "\"deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code\" Pulumi"; top results didn't address the claim. Talk context: https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/
verdicts.framing_note: The only related source found shows that an SST Founding Engineer (Dax Raad) spoke at PulumiUP 2024. It doesn't include the quoted words.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording ("intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things") reads like a paraphrase of a talk rather than a direct quote. Check it against the PulumiUP talk recording before publishing it inside quotation marks.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for infrastructure deployments.
verdicts.evidence: The /product/pulumi-insights/ URL is now an alias that redirects to the Discovery & Governance page. That page does promise visibility: "Pulumi discovers all resources, including those created outside infrastructure-as-code, providing complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting." But what it describes is compliance auditing and resource search, not debugging deployments. The blog credits the debugging benefit to the infrastructure code being the same as the deployment code, which is not what the linked product does.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source offers 'complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting' of cloud resources; the claim says it gives 'improved visibility and debugging capabilities for infrastructure deployments' and treats it as SST's code-tracing benefit
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link anchor points to a product that has since been rebranded as Discovery & Governance, and it doesn't match the benefit the paragraph describes (tracing issues back to the source code).

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.

The claim lists only some of the supported languages, but everything it lists is accurate. On-premises targets such as Kubernetes and VMware are well known through Pulumi's providers, though this page doesn't state it outright.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names four languages; the docs list those four plus JavaScript, Java, YAML, and HCL. Leaving some out doesn't make the claim wrong.

verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for a new SST engine for deploying SST applications, deploying components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable it will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: SST's Jan 2024 post matches the wording: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications... Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3." That forecast is now out of date. SST's Aug 2024 post says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3", so the future-tense framing is stale in a 2026 post. SST also says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi", which the claim leaves out.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the source's Jan 2024 forecast ("once stable, it'll be released as SST v3") is stated as current, but it has already happened (SST v3 shipped Aug 2024). The claim also drops the Terraform-providers part of the source.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Related PR pulumi/docs#21673 moves this FAQ answer to past tense (Ion shipped as SST v3 in Aug 2024; v4 is built on the same engine). If this line still says "will be released", it is stale.

verdicts.text: Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: The sentence copies SST's January 2024 post word for word: "Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3." But that release has already happened. SST's August 20, 2024 post says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3." So the fact is right, but the future tense is now out of date.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: SST's 2024 post describes a planned release ("it'll be released as SST v3"). As of 2026 that release is done ("Ion is now officially SST v3", Aug 2024). The sentence should use past tense, e.g. "Ion was released as SST v3 in August 2024".
verdicts.intuition_flag: A temporal claim written as future tense in a 2026 blog PR, about an event that happened in August 2024.

verdicts.evidence: This is the blog post's front-matter publication date (`date: 2026-09-16`). It is metadata the author sets for their own post, not a factual assertion about anything outside the post, so there is nothing external to check it against.

The quoted mechanism, "translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`", does not appear in the fetched content, so it can't be confirmed.

verdicts.text: Nitric and Defang, like SST, run application deployments through the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-defang README says its CD program "receives a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`". Nitric's cloud/aws go.mod depends on github.com/pulumi/pulumi/sdk/v3 and the Terraform-bridged pulumi-aws, pulumi-random and pulumi-docker SDKs. The same go.mod also pulls in cdktf provider modules, so Nitric has a Terraform deployment path too. That means the Pulumi route covers Nitric's direct deployment providers, not every Nitric deployment.
verdicts.framing_note: Defang's README says it runs `pulumi up`, and Nitric's dependencies are Pulumi and bridged providers. For Nitric, the Pulumi path applies to its direct deployment providers; it also has Terraform (cdktf) providers.

verdicts.text: SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed and its release cadence has not changed because of the opencode work.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi-dependency half holds: third-party write-ups (Encore, Aug 2026) still describe SST v3+ as running on Pulumi. The cadence half is disputed by two independent third-party sources. Northflank (Jan 2026) says "SST development slowed in 2025 after the team shifted focus to OpenCode," and bex.co (Aug 2026) says SST's changelog has been reduced to security bumps. I found no statement from SST itself saying its cadence is unchanged.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim joins an accurate part (still depends on the Pulumi engine) with an unsupported negative causal claim (cadence unchanged by opencode). No cited source backs the second part.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Neither contradicting source is authoritative: both are competitor/third-party blogs. Still, the PR's own notes only show that a v4.17.1 release exists (July 2026), which says nothing about cadence. The author should soften the wording or drop the cadence assertion.

verdicts.intuition_flag: The date range "September 5-11, 2026" is very specific. Check that it's a real week that has already passed and that the figure came from the npm downloads API.

verdicts.text: The opencode work has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

verdicts.text: That's confirmed outside SST's own writing, too. Independent developers who've compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture:
verdicts.evidence: Third-party comparisons that don't come from SST itself describe the same architecture. cdkbase's SST-vs-Terraform article says SST v3 "rebuilt on the Pulumi engine with Terraform providers underneath," and Encore's comparison calls SST "a higher-level layer on top of Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: This line only introduces the claim; the architecture it refers to (SST running on the Pulumi engine with Terraform providers) is spelled out in the quote that follows. Independent comparison pieces (cdkbase, Encore) confirm it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The line doesn't name who the 'independent developers' are. The sources are vendor comparison blogs, not individual developers, so check that the quote that follows is attributed to a specific source.

verdicts.text: Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page loads (HTTP 200) and is Gautier Blandin's article, but the pre-fetched body cuts off partway through the Pulumi section, so the SST passage is missing. The fetched text never says "SST uses the Pulumi engine" or that users can write Pulumi code alongside SST constructs, so I can't quote support for the claim.
verdicts.framing_note: Supporting passage not in the fetched text. Small title difference: the page reads "Terraform vs Pulumi vs SST / A tradeoffs analysis", while the claim has "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis".

verdicts.evidence: The page returned HTTP 200 and confirms the title and author ("headline":"SST Ditches AWS CDK: Time to Move on to Ion", author "Kiryl Anoshka"). The fetched body is cut off in the AWS CDK section, before the Ion/Pulumi imports discussion, so the quoted sentence doesn't appear in what I have and can't be checked.
verdicts.framing_note: Title and author match. The quote itself sits past the truncation point of the pre-fetched body.

verdicts.text: SST's published platform/package.json depends on @pulumi/pulumi plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (@pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls, @pulumiverse/vercel).
verdicts.evidence: The dependencies block of platform/package.json lists "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0", "@pulumi/cloudflare": "6.15.0", "@pulumi/command": "1.0.1", "@pulumi/docker-build": "0.0.14", "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0", "@pulumi/random": "4.16.6", "@pulumi/tls": "5.0.1", "@pulumiverse/vercel": "4.6.0". That matches every package the claim names.
verdicts.framing_note: All seven named Pulumi/Pulumiverse packages plus @pulumi/pulumi appear in "dependencies" of the published file.

verdicts.text: In SST deploys, components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations, and Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: The fetched body is only the repo title: "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That backs the general idea of Terraform-bridged providers. It says nothing about SST components compiling into Pulumi resources, or about the engine diffing state and ordering operations through a dependency graph.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi.' The claim goes further and describes SST's whole deploy pipeline, including engine diffing and the dependency graph.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
verdicts.evidence: This matches how Pulumi's engine is documented. The engine builds the resource dependency graph, runs preview and diff, and tracks state, and it talks to provider plugins over gRPC. Pulumi's own docs index says the registry covers "thousands of cloud providers", so "hundreds" is, if anything, an understatement. That page only backs up the provider count; it is not an independent check of the engine's features.
verdicts.framing_note: Strictly, providers are separate plugins, not part of the engine. But the claim only says the engine provides the "plumbing" to them, which is accurate.

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
verdicts.evidence: AWS's own announcements show resource-type counts in the high hundreds: "CloudFormation now supports 170+ AWS services spanning over 900 resource types" (Apr 2022). A current third-party index lists 1,613 CloudFormation resource types, so "hundreds" is a low estimate but still true as a lower bound.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The current count is over 1,000 (about 1,600 CloudFormation types), so "more than a thousand" would be more accurate than "hundreds".

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi docs list DIY backends alongside Pulumi Cloud: "a 'Do It Yourself' backend that stores state in an object store you manage—AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, ... or your local filesystem." That means the engine can run without a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Pulumi-hosted service" is absolute. By default the CLI downloads plugins from get.pulumi.com and checks for updates, but both can be avoided by pre-installing plugins or turning the checks off. Consider softening the wording.

verdicts.text: The link targets /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exist.
verdicts.evidence: I found a content file for each of the three link targets in the repo: content/blog/any-terraform-provider/index.md (title: "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi"), content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md (title: Automation API) and content/docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers.md (title: Use Terraform Providers).

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, working by embedding the engine without requiring Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: The Automation API docs say it is a "strongly typed SDK, so you can drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application", that it is "part of Pulumi IaC's open source offering", and that it suits "Building higher-level tools, such as custom CLIs over Pulumi". It works with any state backend, so Pulumi Cloud isn't needed. One caveat: the docs also say it "drives the Pulumi CLI under the hood, so the CLI must be available to your program at runtime". That means "embedding the engine" isn't literally in-process.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Embedding the engine" overstates the mechanism a bit: Automation API runs the pulumi CLI as a separate process rather than linking the engine into the program. The author may want to say "drives the engine" instead.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem for the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: The repo describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That backs the main fact, that the bridge lets Terraform providers be used from Pulumi. Nothing on the page says it was built specifically for projects like SST.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the source's general purpose ('allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi') becomes a stated design intent ('built specifically to let projects like SST reuse...').
verdicts.intuition_flag: The bridge mainly exists to power Pulumi's own bridged providers. The claim credits it with a purpose aimed at SST-like projects, which the source doesn't give.

verdicts.text: Most SST users never write Pulumi code; resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's config docs confirm that Pulumi resources can be defined in the same app: the run function "is where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components", and "You can add Pulumi code in the run function." A third-party explainer backs the compile-to-Pulumi part: "Each component you write maps to one or more underlying Pulumi/Terraform resources." The "most users never write Pulumi code" part has no numbers behind it, but it fits SST presenting Pulumi as an internal engine.
verdicts.framing_note: No source is cited, so the claim was checked against SST docs. How it works is confirmed; the "most SST users" usage claim is soft and has no data behind it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Most SST users never write Pulumi code" is a usage claim with no data behind it. Consider softening it (e.g., "many SST users").

verdicts.text: Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi inside an SST app and deployed as part of the same app, because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's official docs say "Aside from the built-in SST components, all the Pulumi/Terraform providers are supported as well," and "Once added, you can use a resource from the provider in your sst.config.ts." They also say a component's nodes are "references to the underlying Pulumi components that are created," which backs up the claim that SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs say any Pulumi/Terraform provider resource can go in sst.config.ts alongside the built-in components, and that SST uses Pulumi as its deployment engine. The claim that such resources deploy as part of the same app follows from that.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud offers cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails enforced centrally, and components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
verdicts.evidence: The link /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/ works: it is an alias of content/docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud.md. That page calls Pulumi Cloud "the default state backend" and says an organization "is the primary unit of collaboration: teams and role-based access control... all belong to an organization." It also lists "Policy as code enforcement applied centrally to every update." Components aren't covered on this page, but the post links a separate /docs/iac/concepts/components/ page for them.
verdicts.framing_note: The linked page describes Pulumi Cloud as a state backend with organization/team collaboration, RBAC, and resource inventory. "Cross-team visibility into infrastructure state" is a fair summary of that. The policy and components parts point to their own linked pages.

verdicts.text: Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own v3 announcement (dated August 20, 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3" and that SST "was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation" before the new engine that "would use Pulumi and Terraform". Other sources confirm that Terraform providers are bridged through Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: "Mid-2024" loosely matches the August 20, 2024 GA post. Ion had been in gradual rollout for months before that.

verdicts.text: SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." Third-party write-ups say SST v3 keeps its state as Pulumi state in an S3 bucket. The negative parts of the claim (no Terraform CLI, no Terraform state) follow from this but aren't stated word for word.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says Pulumi is the engine and Terraform providers are bridged through it. The claim adds the negatives "no Terraform CLI / no Terraform state", which follow from that but aren't in the source's words.

verdicts.text: SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own Console docs say that with it "you and your team can see all your apps, their resources and updates," through shared team workspaces. SST's Basics docs also cover referencing "resources that are managed by a different team," and sharing resources across stages with static `get` methods. So the claims of no cross-team visibility and no shared infrastructure are too strong. Nothing I found shows SST offering policy enforcement.
verdicts.framing_note: This could hold up if "on its own" means only the open-source SST framework without the optional SaaS Console. But the Console is SST's own first-party product, and cross-app resource referencing is in the core framework, so the flat negative claim is still overstated.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a broad negative claim about a competitor that bundles three separate capabilities. Only the policy-enforcement part looks accurate.
